title: Crescent lace shawl
subtitle: An asymmetric crescent in fingering weight with a feather-and-fan bound-off edge.
excerpt: An asymmetric crescent-shaped shawl in fingering-weight wool, cast on at one short end and worked with increases on one edge only to create a curved shape. A feather-and-fan row runs along the bound-off edge as a decorative finish. Wingspan approximately 185 cm, depth approximately 48 cm at the deepest point. About 350 g of fingering yarn.
sourceNotes: The side-to-side asymmetric construction is a modern shawl form. Feather-and-fan as a decorative bound-off band is documented in Mary Thomas's Book of Knitting Patterns (1943). No period source for the combined crescent shape.

knitting.gaugeText: 24 sts × 48 rows = 10 × 10 cm in stockinette on 3.75 mm needles, blocked.
knitting.finishedSizeText: Wingspan approximately 185 cm. Depth at deepest point approximately 48 cm. Blocked.

glossaryTerms.definition: A shawl shape worked from one short tip to the other, with increases only on the top (curved) edge and a straight or decreasing lower edge. The result is a curved crescent when blocked.

content.text: An
asymmetric crescent
shawl in fingering wool, worked from one short tip to the other with upper-edge increases and a feather-and-fan cast-off. Wingspan approximately 185 cm, depth approximately 48 cm.

The side-to-side construction grows the wingspan rather than the depth, giving a long shallow crescent. Increases run along the upper edge every RS row; the lower edge stays straight until the feather-and-fan cast-off. Budget about 350 g (about 1,400 m / 1,530 yards) of fingering wool.
What you need

items.name: Yarn
items.qty: About 350 g (1,400 m / 1,530 yards) of fingering-weight yarn

items.name: Needles
items.qty: 3.75 mm (UK 9 / US 5) circular needle, 100 cm or longer

items.name: Tapestry needle, scissors, blocking mat, pins

content.text: Gauge

24 stitches and 48 rows to 10 cm over stockinette on 3.75 mm needles, blocked. If your blocked gauge reads 26 stitches per 10 cm, the wingspan at the same stitch count will be about 171 cm rather than 185 cm. For the crescent shape the depth is more sensitive to gauge: 2 extra stitches per 10 cm compresses the depth by about 5 cm at the deepest point.
Stitches used
Pattern
Cast on
Using the long-tail cast-on, cast on 4 stitches. For the long-tail, leave a tail of approximately (3.75 × 4) / 10 + 15 = 16.5 cm before the slip knot.
Set-up rows
Rows 1 to 4: k all sts. On row 3 (RS), place a marker after st 2. The marker divides the upper edge from the lower edge.
Body
RS row: k to marker, yo, SM, k to end. (1 stitch added on the upper edge each RS row)
WS row: k3, p to 3 sts before end, k3. (garter selvedge on each long edge)
Continue until the wingspan reaches about 185 cm. The upper edge holds about 446 stitches at that point.
Feather-and-fan finish
Before binding off, work a feather-and-fan row. The row alternates decreases and yarn-overs in a wave, creating a scallop along the cast-off edge.
Work Jeny's surprisingly stretchy bind-off on the following RS row. The scallop edge needs stretch to sit flat when blocked.
Stitch count check-ins
After 100 RS rows: 4 + 100 = 104 stitches. Wingspan approximately 43 cm. The crescent curve should be visible when the work is laid flat.
After 250 RS rows: 4 + 250 = 254 stitches. Wingspan approximately 106 cm. Nearly halfway to the full wingspan.
Common faults
Increases worked on both edges: the crescent shape depends on only one edge growing. Check every RS row that the yarn-over increase is placed at the marker only, not at the lower selvedge.

Crescent points uneven after blocking: the two short ends were cast on and cast off at different tensions. Both short ends should be about the same 4-stitch width. If one spreads more than the other under pin tension, the crescent will not drape symmetrically.
Scallop edge puckering after blocking: the feather-and-fan bind-off row was too tight. Work the bind-off row on a needle one size larger to keep the scallop open.
Blocking

Soak for 15 minutes in cool water, press out in towels. Block the crescent by pinning the two short tips first, then the centre of the upper curved edge. Pin the lower edge in a gentle curve. The crescent shape deepens with aggressive pinning: pin the upper edge in a shallow curve for a crescent that lies flat, or pin it in a more pronounced arch for a deeper crescent.
Care
Hand wash in cool water, lay flat to dry. Re-block when the crescent curve relaxes after wearing.
What to try next

A crescent with a deeper body can be made by adding a double increase (two yarn overs at the marker) every other RS row instead of one. This produces a crescent with a shallower wingspan-to-depth ratio and a more dramatic curve on the upper edge.
